items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “a focused question that guides an investigation and can be answered using evidence”.
items.answer: Enquiry question
items.markingKey: Enquiry question: a focused question that guides an investigation and can be answered using evidence. [1]

items.stem: Explain why an enquiry question should be focused rather than very broad.
items.answer: A focused question tells the investigator exactly what data to collect and can be answered within the time and resources available; a broad question cannot be answered properly with evidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: guides data collection; 1 mark: can be answered with available time/evidence [2]

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using a questionnaire to find out people’s views.
items.answer: Advantage: it can collect answers from many people quickly and closed questions are easy to compare. Disadvantage: people may not answer honestly or may misunderstand questions; response rates can be low.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for an explained advantage and disadvantage [2]

items.stem: A class in Lima is investigating whether a new shopping mall on the edge of town has affected small shops in the town centre. Explain how the students could choose a fair sample.
items.answer: Use random or systematic sampling (e.g. every 5th person or site at regular intervals) and collect enough data at different times/places so the sample is representative.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named sampling method; 1 mark explained fairness/representativeness [2]

items.stem: A group in Jakarta is investigating how the local river changes from its source to its mouth. (a) Write a suitable hypothesis for this investigation. (b) Identify one ethical or safety issue the students should consider, and how to deal with it.
items.answer: (a) The river becomes wider and deeper further downstream. (b) Ask permission and keep answers anonymous; work in groups, wear high-visibility clothing near roads or water and tell a teacher where they are.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark testable statement linked to the enquiry [1] (b) 1 mark issue; 1 mark way of managing it [2]

items.stem: Isla argues that primary data is always more useful than secondary data in a humanities investigation. To what extent do you agree? Give reasons for and against before reaching a judgement. You may wish to consider: reliability of who collected the data; sample size; time periods.
items.answer: Agree: Primary data is collected for the exact question and is up to date. The investigator knows how it was collected, so its reliability can be judged. Disagree: Secondary data such as a census covers far more people and places than a student could survey. Secondary data gives change over time (e.g. past maps or records) that cannot be collected now. Primary data from small samples may be unrepresentative. Judgement: Usefulness depends on the question; the best enquiries combine both kinds and cross-check them.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Explain why investigators often use both primary and secondary data.
items.answer: Primary data is up to date and collected for the exact question; secondary data gives a wider picture or a longer time period that the investigator could not collect alone, and allows comparison.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: value of primary; 1 mark: value of secondary/comparison [2]

items.stem: Students in Santiago are investigating how life in their town changed after the railway arrived in the 19th century. (a) Write a suitable hypothesis for this investigation. (b) Suggest two methods of collecting primary data for this investigation. (c) Suggest how the results could be presented, giving a reason.
items.answer: (a) The railway caused the town’s population and number of factories to grow. (b) Interviewing a local historian; photographing old buildings near the station. (c) A line graph of population and a pair of maps from before and after the railway, because it shows the pattern clearly and allows comparison.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark testable statement linked to the enquiry [1] (b) 1 mark each appropriate method [2] (c) 1 mark suitable presentation; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “a source produced at the time of the events being studied, often by someone who was there”.
items.answer: Primary source
items.markingKey: Primary source: a source produced at the time of the events being studied, often by someone who was there. [1]

items.stem: Explain why a primary source is not always more reliable than a secondary source.
items.answer: A primary source may be biased, limited to one viewpoint or written for propaganda; a secondary source can draw on many sources with hindsight, so may be more balanced.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness of primary (bias/limited view); 1 mark: strength of secondary (range/hindsight) [2]

items.stem: Explain how the purpose of a source can affect its reliability.
items.answer: If a source was made to persuade (e.g. propaganda or an advert) it may exaggerate or leave out facts, so it is less reliable as evidence of what happened, though it is good evidence of what its author wanted people to believe.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: persuasive purpose → selective/exaggerated; 1 mark: still useful for attitudes/aims [2]

items.stem: Read Source A carefully. “We start at half past five and the overlooker beats any child who falls asleep. My fingers bleed from the threads and there is never enough light or air.” (A diary kept by a 14-year-old cotton mill worker in Manchester, 1833 (adapted).) Suggest the purpose of Source A. Explain your answer.
items.answer: To record the writer’s own daily experiences, probably for herself or her family rather than to persuade.
items.markingKey: 1 mark purpose; 1 mark link to author/audience/date [2]

items.stem: Study Source C, a diary kept by a 14-year-old cotton mill worker in Manchester, 1833 (adapted). “We start at half past five and the overlooker beats any child who falls asleep. My fingers bleed from the threads and there is never enough light or air.” (a) Suggest the purpose of Source C. Explain your answer. (b) Use your own knowledge to describe one aspect of working conditions in textile mills that Source C does not show.
items.answer: (a) To record the writer’s own daily experiences, probably for herself or her family rather than to persuade. (b) How many hours were allowed by law or how conditions changed after the 1833 Factory Act.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark purpose; 1 mark link to author/audience/date [2] (b) 1 mark accurate own knowledge; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: Read Source B carefully. “We start at half past five and the overlooker beats any child who falls asleep. My fingers bleed from the threads and there is never enough light or air.” (A diary kept by a 14-year-old cotton mill worker in Manchester, 1833 (adapted).) (a) Is Source B a primary or a secondary source? Give a reason for your answer. (b) What can you infer from Source B about working conditions in textile mills?
items.answer: (a) Primary source: it comes from the time being studied, or from someone directly involved in the events. (b) Conditions were harsh: very long hours, physical punishment and injuries were common for child workers.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct type; 1 mark reason based on its origin/date [2] (b) 1 mark valid inference; 1 mark supported with a detail from the source [2]

items.stem: Study Source B, a diary kept by a 14-year-old cotton mill worker in Manchester, 1833 (adapted). “We start at half past five and the overlooker beats any child who falls asleep. My fingers bleed from the threads and there is never enough light or air.” (a) Is Source B a primary or a secondary source? Give a reason for your answer. (b) Use your own knowledge to describe one aspect of working conditions in textile mills that Source B does not show.
items.answer: (a) Primary source: it comes from the time being studied, or from someone directly involved in the events. (b) How many hours were allowed by law or how conditions changed after the 1833 Factory Act.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct type; 1 mark reason based on its origin/date [2] (b) 1 mark accurate own knowledge; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: Study Source D, a diary kept by a 14-year-old cotton mill worker in Manchester, 1833 (adapted). “We start at half past five and the overlooker beats any child who falls asleep. My fingers bleed from the threads and there is never enough light or air.” (a) What can you infer from Source D about working conditions in textile mills? (b) Use your own knowledge to describe one aspect of working conditions in textile mills that Source D does not show.
items.answer: (a) Conditions were harsh: very long hours, physical punishment and injuries were common for child workers. (b) How many hours were allowed by law or how conditions changed after the 1833 Factory Act.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark valid inference; 1 mark supported with a detail from the source [2] (b) 1 mark accurate own knowledge; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “A source written by someone who was there is always reliable.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Eyewitnesses may be biased, see only part of the events, misremember, or write to persuade.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: A student is given a historian writing in 2005 about the British Empire in India: “British rule brought railways, telegraphs and universities to India, but they were built mainly to serve British trade and administration, and Indian industries such as hand-weaving declined.” What type of source is this?
options: It cannot be classified without a date
Neither: it is an opinion, not a source
items.answer: Secondary source
items.markingKey: Secondary: judged by its origin and date of production, not by whether it is accurate. [1]

items.stem: A student investigating child labour in the 1830s finds Source B. Source B: a school textbook about the Industrial Revolution, published in 2015. “Historians estimate that children made up a large share of the workforce in early cotton mills. Many worked twelve hours or more a day before the Factory Acts.” (a) What can you infer from Source B about child labour in early factories? (b) Suggest the purpose of Source B. Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Child labour was widespread and hours were long before the law was changed. (b) To inform students with a clear overview based on historians’ research.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark valid inference; 1 mark supported with a detail from the source [2] (b) 1 mark purpose; 1 mark link to author/audience/date [2]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “a vertical grid line on a map, numbered from west to east and read first in a grid reference”.
items.answer: Easting
items.markingKey: Easting: a vertical grid line on a map, numbered from west to east and read first in a grid reference. [1]

items.stem: Explain why a six-figure grid reference is more useful than a four-figure grid reference for finding a building.
items.answer: A four-figure reference only gives the 1 km square; a six-figure reference divides the square into tenths and locates a point to within 100 m.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: 4-fig = whole square; 1 mark: 6-fig = point within 100 m [2]

items.stem: Explain how you can tell from contour lines whether a slope is steep or gentle.
items.answer: Close-together contours mean a large change in height over a short distance (steep); widely spaced contours mean a gentle slope.
items.markingKey: 1 mark close = steep; 1 mark wide = gentle [2]

items.stem: On a 1:50 000 map, the castle lies in the grid square whose bottom-left corner is where easting 74 meets northing 77. The symbol is 7 tenths of the way across the square (eastwards) and 2 tenths of the way up (northwards). Give (a) the four-figure and (b) the six-figure grid reference of the castle.
items.markingKey: (a) 7477 [1] (b) 747772: easting first, then northing [1]

items.stem: On a 1:50 000 map, the church lies in the grid square whose bottom-left corner is where easting 32 meets northing 73. The symbol is 6 tenths of the way across the square (eastwards) and 9 tenths of the way up (northwards). A castle is at the bottom-left corner of square 3374. The grid squares are 1 km wide. (a) Give the six-figure reference of the church. (b) State the general direction of the castle from the church. (c) Estimate the straight-line distance between them to the nearest 0.5 km.
items.answer: (a) 326739 (b) north-east (c) about 0.5 km
items.markingKey: (a) 326739 [1]; (b) north-east: further east and north [1]; (c) Pythagoras on the grid or measured with ruler, ±0.5 km [1]

items.stem: Hana argues that digital maps and satellite navigation have made paper maps and map skills unnecessary. To what extent do you agree? Give reasons for and against before reaching a judgement. You may wish to consider: remote areas; reliability of technology; interpreting relief.
items.answer: Agree: Digital maps update quickly, can zoom and show live traffic or hazards. Satellite navigation calculates routes automatically. Disagree: Phones lose signal or battery in remote areas, so walkers and emergency teams still need paper maps. Map skills (grid references, contours, scale) are needed to interpret any map, including digital ones. GIS still uses the same ideas of scale, layers and location. Judgement: Digital tools have changed how maps are used, but map skills remain essential to understand and check them.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Explain the difference between a large-scale and a small-scale map, with an example of a use for each.
items.answer: Large-scale (e.g. 1:10 000) shows a small area in detail, useful for a town walk; small-scale (e.g. 1:1 000 000) shows a large area with little detail, useful for a country road map.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each type with suitable use [2]

items.stem: How far do you agree that digital maps and satellite navigation have made paper maps and map skills unnecessary? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
items.answer: Agree: Digital maps update quickly, can zoom and show live traffic or hazards. Satellite navigation calculates routes automatically. Disagree: Phones lose signal or battery in remote areas, so walkers and emergency teams still need paper maps. Map skills (grid references, contours, scale) are needed to interpret any map, including digital ones. GIS still uses the same ideas of scale, layers and location. Judgement: Digital tools have changed how maps are used, but map skills remain essential to understand and check them.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the average found by adding all the values and dividing by the number of values”.
items.answer: Mean
items.markingKey: Mean: the average found by adding all the values and dividing by the number of values. [1]

items.stem: Explain why the median is sometimes a better average than the mean.
items.answer: The median is not affected by one or two extreme values (anomalies), so it can better represent a typical value in uneven data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: median = middle value; 1 mark: not distorted by extremes [2]

items.stem: Explain why a scatter graph showing a correlation does not prove that one variable causes the other.
items.answer: Both may be linked to a third factor, or the relationship may be coincidence; correlation only shows that they change together.
items.markingKey: 1 mark third factor/coincidence; 1 mark correlation ≠ causation [2]

items.stem: A student recorded the number of daily rainfall in mm on 7 days: Mon 40, Tue 42, Wed 46, Thu 55, Fri 28, Sat 58, Sun 50. Calculate the mean to one decimal place.

A student recorded the number of pedestrians counted in 10 minutes at 5 sites: A 49, B 45, C 14, D 30, E 20. (a) Calculate the range. (b) Suggest a suitable graph to present this data and give a reason.
items.answer: (a) 35 (b) A bar chart, because the data is for separate (discrete) categories, so values can be compared easily.
items.markingKey: (a) 49 − 14 = 35 [1] (b) 1 mark graph; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Diego argues that a climate graph tells us everything we need to know about the climate of a place. To what extent do you agree? Give reasons for and against before reaching a judgement.
items.answer: Agree: It shows monthly temperature and precipitation, the annual range and the wet and dry seasons. Disagree: It shows averages, hiding extremes such as heatwaves, storms and droughts. It does not show wind, humidity, sunshine hours or daily (diurnal) range. It may not show recent climate change or variation within the area. Judgement: It is a very useful summary but needs other data to give a full picture.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: A student recorded the number of pedestrians counted in 10 minutes at 5 sites: A 24, B 60, C 22, D 4, E 36. What is the range of the data?

The table shows climate data for Town S. Temperature (°C): Jan 25, Feb 25.5, Mar 27, Apr 28.5, May 29, Jun 29, Jul 28.5, Aug 27, Sep 27.5, Oct 28, Nov 28, Dec 26.5. Precipitation (mm): Jan 1, Feb 1, Mar 0, Apr 1, May 15, Jun 500, Jul 840, Aug 560, Sep 330, Oct 70, Nov 15, Dec 2. (a) Calculate the total annual precipitation. (b) Identify the wettest month and give its rainfall.
items.answer: (a) 2335 mm (b) July, 840 mm
items.markingKey: (a) sum of the 12 months = 2335 mm [2] (b) [1]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “a summary of what the evidence shows, answering the enquiry question”.
items.answer: Conclusion
items.markingKey: Conclusion: a summary of what the evidence shows, answering the enquiry question. [1]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “a judgement on the strengths and weaknesses of the methods, data and conclusions”.
items.answer: Evaluation
items.markingKey: Evaluation: a judgement on the strengths and weaknesses of the methods, data and conclusions. [1]

items.stem: Explain why it is important to identify limitations in an investigation.
items.answer: It shows how far the conclusion can be trusted and helps suggest improvements for future investigations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark trust in conclusion; 1 mark improvements [2]

items.stem: A student tested the hypothesis “Most residents think the new park has improved the area.” In a survey of 40 residents, 20 said yes. All the interviews were done at the park entrance on a Sunday. Identify one limitation of the data and explain how it affects the conclusion.
items.answer: Data collected only once/at one place and time (e.g. one weekday morning or at the park entrance on a Sunday), so it may not be representative and the conclusion is tentative.
items.markingKey: 1 mark limitation; 1 mark effect [2]

items.stem: Explain whether you agree that the most important part of an enquiry is collecting a large amount of data. Give one reason for and one reason against.
items.answer: Agree: More data makes results more representative and reliable. Disagree: Data must be accurate and relevant to the question; lots of poor data is still poor. A good question and careful analysis are needed to reach a valid conclusion. Evaluation shows how far conclusions can be trusted. Judgement: Quantity helps, but the quality of the question, method, analysis and evaluation matters as much.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1 mark): one simple reason. Level 2 (2-3 marks): one explained reason for AND one against, with accurate detail.

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “a statement or prediction that can be tested by collecting evidence”.
items.answer: Hypothesis
items.markingKey: Hypothesis: a statement or prediction that can be tested by collecting evidence. [1]

items.stem: Explain why it is important to ask permission and keep answers anonymous when interviewing people.
items.answer: It is ethical: people have a right to privacy and to choose to take part; anonymity also encourages honest answers and protects people from harm.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: ethics/consent/privacy; 1 mark: effect on honesty or protection [2]

items.stem: A class in Cairo is investigating whether a new shopping mall on the edge of town has affected small shops in the town centre. Explain how the students could choose a fair sample.
items.answer: Use random or systematic sampling (e.g. every 5th person or site at regular intervals) and collect enough data at different times/places so the sample is representative.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named sampling method; 1 mark explained fairness/representativeness [2]

items.stem: “A questionnaire is the best way to find out people’s views on a local issue.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: honesty of answers; open and closed questions.
items.answer: Agree: It reaches many people quickly. Closed questions give data that is easy to compare and graph. Disagree: People may not answer honestly or may misunderstand questions. Interviews give more detailed reasons. Who is asked (sampling) matters more than the method itself. Judgement: A questionnaire is useful but works best alongside interviews and a carefully chosen sample.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “a source produced after the events, usually by someone who used other sources to interpret them”.
items.answer: Secondary source
items.markingKey: Secondary source: a source produced after the events, usually by someone who used other sources to interpret them. [1]

items.stem: Explain why an unreliable source can still be useful to a historian.
items.answer: It shows the attitudes, opinions or propaganda of its author and the time it was made, which is useful for questions about views and motives.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: shows attitudes/purpose; 1 mark: linked to a suitable enquiry [2]

items.stem: Source D is taken from a school textbook about the Industrial Revolution, published in 2015. It says: “Historians estimate that children made up a large share of the workforce in early cotton mills. Many worked twelve hours or more a day before the Factory Acts.” Use it to answer the questions. Use your own knowledge to describe one aspect of child labour in early factories that Source D does not show.
items.answer: Individual experiences such as punishments or injuries in a particular mill.
items.markingKey: 1 mark accurate own knowledge; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: Source D is taken from a school textbook about the Industrial Revolution, published in 2015. It says: “Historians estimate that children made up a large share of the workforce in early cotton mills. Many worked twelve hours or more a day before the Factory Acts.” Use it to answer the questions. (a) What can you infer from Source D about child labour in early factories? (b) Use your own knowledge to describe one aspect of child labour in early factories that Source D does not show.
items.answer: (a) Child labour was widespread and hours were long before the law was changed. (b) Individual experiences such as punishments or injuries in a particular mill.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark valid inference; 1 mark supported with a detail from the source [2] (b) 1 mark accurate own knowledge; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: Source B is taken from a letter from a mill owner to a newspaper, Lancashire, 1832 (adapted). It says: “The children in my mill are well fed and cheerful. Work keeps them out of mischief, and their wages help their families. Any law limiting their hours will ruin our trade.” Use it to answer the questions. (a) Is Source B a primary or a secondary source? Give a reason for your answer. (b) What can you infer from Source B about attitudes of factory owners to reform?
items.answer: (a) Primary source: it comes from the time being studied, or from someone directly involved in the events. (b) Some mill owners opposed factory reform and claimed children benefited from work.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct type; 1 mark reason based on its origin/date [2] (b) 1 mark valid inference; 1 mark supported with a detail from the source [2]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “easting”?
options: A vertical grid line on a map, numbered from west to east and read first in a grid reference.
A horizontal grid line on a map, numbered from south to north and read second in a grid reference.
A line on a map joining places of equal height above sea level.
The ratio between a distance on a map and the real distance on the ground.
items.answer: A vertical grid line on a map, numbered from west to east and read first in a grid reference.
items.markingKey: Easting: a vertical grid line on a map, numbered from west to east and read first in a grid reference. [1]

items.stem: Describe how to measure the length of a winding road on a map.
items.answer: Lay a piece of string (or the edge of paper, marking each bend) along the road, then straighten it against the scale line to convert to real distance.
items.markingKey: 1 mark method; 1 mark conversion using scale [2]

items.stem: On a 1:25 000 map, a footpath from the school to the bridge measures 3.5 cm. Calculate the real length of the footpath in kilometres. Show your working.
“Grid references are the most important map skill for a geographer.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion.
items.answer: Agree: They give precise locations, so features can be found, recorded and shared accurately. Disagree: Scale and distance are needed to plan routes and compare sizes. Reading contours shows relief, which matters for hazards, farming and walking routes. Direction and bearings are essential for navigation. Judgement: Grid references are essential, but they are most useful combined with scale, direction and relief.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: A student writes: “The range tells you the average value of a data set.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. The range is the difference between the highest and lowest values; it shows spread, not average.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why climate graphs use averages taken over about 30 years.
items.answer: Weather varies from year to year; averaging over a long period removes unusual years and shows the typical climate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark weather varies; 1 mark long-term average shows typical pattern [2]

items.stem: The table shows climate data for Station P. Temperature (°C): Jan 9, Feb 11.5, Mar 13.5, Apr 14.5, May 18, Jun 23, Jul 25, Aug 26.5, Sep 23, Oct 20, Nov 14, Dec 11.5. Precipitation (mm): Jan 55, Feb 45, Mar 40, Apr 35, May 20, Jun 8, Jul 3, Aug 4, Sep 10, Oct 45, Nov 55, Dec 65. Describe how this data would be drawn on a climate graph.
items.answer: Temperature as a line graph (left axis, °C) and precipitation as bars (right axis, mm), with months along the bottom.
items.markingKey: 1 mark line for temperature; 1 mark bars for precipitation [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that a climate graph tells us everything we need to know about the climate of a place. You may wish to consider: change over time; averages and extremes; other elements of weather.
items.answer: Agree: It shows monthly temperature and precipitation, the annual range and the wet and dry seasons. Disagree: It shows averages, hiding extremes such as heatwaves, storms and droughts. It does not show wind, humidity, sunshine hours or daily (diurnal) range. It may not show recent climate change or variation within the area. Judgement: It is a very useful summary but needs other data to give a full picture.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: A student writes: “If the results do not support the hypothesis, the investigation has failed.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Rejecting a hypothesis is a valid finding; the conclusion explains why the evidence went the other way.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: A student tested the hypothesis “Most residents think the new park has improved the area.” In a survey of 80 residents, 63 said yes. All the interviews were done at the park entrance on a Sunday. Suggest two improvements to make the conclusion more reliable.
items.answer: Repeat on different days and times; increase the sample/sites; use systematic sampling; compare with secondary data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: “The most important part of an enquiry is collecting a large amount of data.” How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. You may wish to consider: the enquiry question; quality versus quantity; analysis and evaluation.
items.answer: Agree: More data makes results more representative and reliable. Disagree: Data must be accurate and relevant to the question; lots of poor data is still poor. A good question and careful analysis are needed to reach a valid conclusion. Evaluation shows how far conclusions can be trusted. Judgement: Quantity helps, but the quality of the question, method, analysis and evaluation matters as much.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “information collected first-hand by the investigator, for example by a survey, count or measurement”.
items.answer: Primary data
items.markingKey: Primary data: information collected first-hand by the investigator, for example by a survey, count or measurement. [1]

items.stem: Explain why a larger sample usually gives more reliable results.
items.answer: A larger sample is more likely to represent the whole population, so a few unusual answers have less effect on the results.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: more representative; 1 mark: reduces effect of anomalies [2]

items.stem: A group in Doha is investigating how a local memorial is used to remember people who died in war. Suggest how the results could be presented, giving a reason.
items.answer: A bar chart of visitors by day and a short set of quotations, because it shows the pattern clearly and allows comparison.
items.markingKey: 1 mark suitable presentation; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: A group in Kathmandu is investigating how a local memorial is used to remember people who died in war. Their hypothesis is: “The memorial is mainly visited on Remembrance Day.” They collected data from 8 people on one Saturday morning. (a) Identify two weaknesses in the way the data was collected. (b) Explain why the students should also use secondary data.
items.answer: (a) The sample of 8 is small and was collected on one Saturday morning, so it may not represent other times or groups of people. (b) Newspaper reports of past ceremonies and the names list from the war graves records would let them check (cross-reference) their own results and see change over a longer period.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each weakness [2] (b) 1 mark source/role; 1 mark explanation [2]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the origin of a source: who produced it, when, where and why”.
items.answer: Provenance
items.markingKey: Provenance: the origin of a source: who produced it, when, where and why. [1]

items.stem: Explain why the date of a source matters when judging its reliability.
items.answer: A source made at the time may be from an eyewitness but lack hindsight; one made much later may suffer from faulty memory or be influenced by later events, but can use more evidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each point [2]

items.stem: Read Source C carefully. “The children in my mill are well fed and cheerful. Work keeps them out of mischief, and their wages help their families. Any law limiting their hours will ruin our trade.” (A letter from a mill owner to a newspaper, Lancashire, 1832 (adapted).) What can you infer from Source C about attitudes of factory owners to reform?
items.answer: Some mill owners opposed factory reform and claimed children benefited from work.
items.markingKey: 1 mark valid inference; 1 mark supported with a detail from the source [2]

items.stem: Study Source C, a recruitment poster issued by the British government in 1914. “Your country needs YOU. Join your country’s army! God save the King.” (a) What can you infer from Source C about how the British government encouraged men to join the army in 1914? (b) Use your own knowledge to describe one aspect of how the British government encouraged men to join the army in 1914 that Source C does not show.
items.answer: (a) The government relied on volunteers and used patriotic, personal appeals to persuade men to enlist. (b) How many men actually joined, or why conscription was introduced in 1916.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark valid inference; 1 mark supported with a detail from the source [2] (b) 1 mark accurate own knowledge; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: Study Source B, an interview with a survivor of the 2015 Nepal earthquake, recorded by a charity in 2016 (adapted). “Our village above Gorkha was cut off for nine days because landslides blocked the road. Helicopters brought rice and tarpaulins, but the monsoon came before we could rebuild.” (a) Suggest the purpose of Source B. Explain your answer. (b) Use your own knowledge to describe one aspect of the effects of the 2015 Nepal earthquake on rural areas that Source B does not show.
items.answer: (a) To record survivors’ experiences, possibly to raise awareness and funds for the charity’s work. (b) Overall figures such as the number of deaths (about 9000) or the effects in Kathmandu.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark purpose; 1 mark link to author/audience/date [2] (b) 1 mark accurate own knowledge; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “northing”?
options: A horizontal grid line on a map, numbered from south to north and read second in a grid reference.
The ratio between a distance on a map and the real distance on the ground.
A dot on a map with a number showing the exact height of that point in metres.
The shape and height of the land.
items.answer: A horizontal grid line on a map, numbered from south to north and read second in a grid reference.
items.markingKey: Northing: a horizontal grid line on a map, numbered from south to north and read second in a grid reference. [1]

items.stem: Explain why satellite images and maps are often used together.
items.answer: Satellite images show what the land actually looks like now (e.g. land use, flooding), while maps add names, symbols, heights and grid references for exact location.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: On a map with a contour interval of 20 m, point X lies on the 50 m contour and point Y, on a hilltop, lies on the 110 m contour. The horizontal distance from X to Y is 600 m. (a) Calculate the difference in height between X and Y. (b) State how many contour lines you would cross walking from X to Y (not counting the one at X).

“Digital maps and satellite navigation have made paper maps and map skills unnecessary.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: interpreting relief; reliability of technology; remote areas.
items.answer: Agree: Digital maps update quickly, can zoom and show live traffic or hazards. Satellite navigation calculates routes automatically. Disagree: Phones lose signal or battery in remote areas, so walkers and emergency teams still need paper maps. Map skills (grid references, contours, scale) are needed to interpret any map, including digital ones. GIS still uses the same ideas of scale, layers and location. Judgement: Digital tools have changed how maps are used, but map skills remain essential to understand and check them.

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “A line graph is suitable for showing data that changes continuously over time.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. The line joins points in sequence to show trends over time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using a choropleth map.
items.answer: Advantage: shows patterns across areas clearly at a glance. Disadvantage: assumes the value is the same across each whole area and hides variation within areas; boundaries are sharp.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: In a survey, 180 people were asked about the main reason for their visit. Results: very safe 35, safe 31, unsafe 18, very unsafe 96. Calculate the percentage of people who answered “very safe”, to one decimal place.

“Choosing the right type of graph is the most important part of presenting data.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: labelling and scales; data accuracy; interpretation.
items.answer: Agree: The right graph makes patterns clear; the wrong one can hide or distort them. Disagree: Accurate data collection matters more: a good graph of poor data is still misleading. Clear labelling, scales and a key are equally important. Interpretation with figures turns a graph into evidence. Judgement: Graph choice matters a great deal, but accuracy, labelling and interpretation are just as important.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “A conclusion should include figures from the results.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Data gives evidence for the judgement and makes it precise.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: A student tested the hypothesis “Traffic is heavier near the town centre than on the edge of town.” Counts of vehicles in one hour: near the centre 296, on the edge of town 236. Data was collected once, on a weekday morning. Write a supported conclusion of two sentences for this enquiry.
items.answer: Supported: the centre had 296 vehicles and the edge 236, a difference of 60 (25.4% of the lower value). However, because of the small, one-off sample the conclusion should be treated with caution.
items.markingKey: 1 mark answer to hypothesis with evidence; 1 mark reflection/qualification [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that an investigation that disproves its hypothesis has failed. You may wish to consider: testing ideas; reliability; what counts as success.
items.answer: Agree: The investigator did not find the expected pattern. Disagree: A rejected hypothesis is still new knowledge. The conclusion can explain why the result was different. Science and humanities enquiries both progress by testing and rejecting ideas. Judgement: Disagree: an investigation succeeds if it answers the question with reliable evidence, whatever the result.
